newsitem.title: USA: Rough Mississippi River hampers grain loadings.
newsitem.headline: Rough Mississippi River hampers grain loadings.

text.p: Grain loadings at New Orleans have been substantially delayed in recent weeks, hampered by rising floodwaters and a string of mishaps on the flood-swollen Mississsippi River, shipping sources said.
"People are having trouble getting cargo delivered to the elevators," said one shipbroker. "The whole process is being disrupted."

High water levels and swift currents have forced operators to take unusual measures to secure barges at the elevators during loading, adding to the time it takes to switch cargo to the elevators, and from there to larger vessels for export.
The biggest elevators along the river were reportedly experiencing backlogs of anywhere from several days to two weeks.
"It's difficult to move tows around with this kind of current," said Matt Boucree, operations manager with Blue Water Shipping in New Orleans. "Moving barges into elevators has been a problem."
Coast Guard-imposed delays farther upriver have added to the backlog.

Traffic has been restricted at various points along the Mississippi since early last week, when a barge tow plowed into the Interstate 90 bridge near Baton Rouge, Louisiana. Vessels have been limited to one-way, one-at-a-time transit in the area since then, and the Coast Guard placed additional requirements on barge size-to-horsepower ratios.
Even those restrictions failed to prevent several more barge accidents on the fast-moving river, including one on Tuesday in which a freighter collided with a tow of 24 barges.
Further complicating the situation on the river, shipping sources said, is an ongoing outage at one of the biggest grain elevators in the U.S. Gulf.

Loadings at Zen-Noh Grain Corp's Convent, Louisiana, export facility have been halted since late February, when a grain freighter crashed into one of the plant's four loading towers. Zen-Noh officials have stated that repairs at the Convent facility will take "several months", though some industry traders do not expect the plant to be back on-line until mid-summer.
"We really see the effect of Zen-Noh being out of the loop now," another shipbroker said. "All of the ships that would be loaded by Zen-Noh have to be taken care of by other elevators."
Arthur Daniels Midland Co has picked up much of the slack for Zen-Noh, traders said, causing delays at ADM's three U.S. Gulf elevators. ADM officials were unable to comment.
While operations headaches abound for operators along the Mississippi, dealers said the chaos has had little impact on the flow of U.S. grain exports.
"Exports are so slow right now that they're almost non-affected," said one grain exporter. "There is still enough of supply south of the traffic delay to meet the demand."

Some shipbrokers said the shortage of cargo in the Mississippi could force freight rates higher, especially on the U.S. Gulf-Far East route, but they cautioned that a general slowdown of business ahead of the Easter holiday made market conditions difficult to assess.
((-- W Pollack, New York Commodities Desk +1 212 859 1640))
